title: Why a polynomial can pretend to be eˣ
mystery: How can one point know the whole curve?
picture: A smooth curve carries enough information at a single point to rebuild itself.

cards.text: How can one point know the whole curve?

Hold that question. The road to it starts somewhere unglamorous — with an awkward truth nobody mentions: **you cannot actually compute $e^x$.** Not by hand, not with gears, not with a chip. Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division — that is the whole toolkit. Everything else has to be built from those four.

And yet somebody has to. A ship's navigator needs $\sin$ of an angle to five decimals or she runs aground. So for three centuries, the most valuable question in applied mathematics was brutally practical: *how do you compute a curve you cannot compute?*
The answer was to find an impostor. Something built only from $+$, $-$, $\times$ — a **polynomial** — that behaves so much like the real function that nobody can tell the difference.

A straight line can imitate a curve for an instant.
A parabola imitates it a little longer.
A cubic survives longer still.

cards.caption: Raise the degree. Watch how far the imitation holds.

cards.text: Each extra derivative is another promise: *I will behave like the real function just a little farther.* Match the value — the curves touch. Match the slope — they travel together. Match the bend, and the bend of the bend, and the impostor clings on through territory it had no right to reach.

cards.caption: Never stop making promises, and the impostor stops pretending. It *becomes* the function.

cards.text: Now notice what just happened, because it should disturb you slightly.
cards.text2: Every coefficient came from derivatives **at a single point** — at $x=0$, and nowhere else. We never looked at what $e^x$ does at $x=2$. We never had to.

cards.text: Taylor published the recipe as a piece of technique. It took another generation to feel the vertigo in it: a smooth function keeps no secrets. Examine it under a microscope at *one* location — its value, its slope, its curvature, forever — and you have recovered the whole curve, out to the horizon.

That is why this idea earns a room of its own. It is not a trick for computing $e^{0.3}$. It is the discovery that **local information can be total information** — and it is why your exam keeps asking you to replace a monstrous limit with three friendly terms and watch it collapse.
A smooth curve carries enough information at a single point to rebuild itself.
Take $\cos x$ and write its first three promises: match the value at $0$, then the slope, then the bend. You will get $1 - x^2/2$ — and you will have computed a cosine with nothing but arithmetic.
